description: Analyze losses instead of wins: interview prospects who chose someone else to find the real reason. Win analysis tells you what you already know. Loss analysis reveals gaps you cannot see.

steps.description: Identify 10-15 recent lost deals where you reached the proposal or negotiation stage (early-stage drops are less informative).

inputs.name: deal-history
inputs.desc: Recent deals that were lost, with the stage at which they were lost and the stated reason

outputs.name: interview-candidates
outputs.desc: 10-15 lost deals where you reached late stage, with contact info for the decision maker

outputs.name: stated-reasons
outputs.desc: The reason each deal was lost according to your CRM or sales team

process: Pull all deals lost in the past 6-12 months. Filter to those that reached the proposal, negotiation, or decision stage. Early-stage drops are usually about fit, not about your weaknesses.

Record the stated loss reason from your CRM. These are almost always wrong or incomplete because they are recorded by the salesperson, not the buyer. Common fake reasons: 'price too high' (often means value was unclear), 'went with incumbent' (often means switching cost was not addressed).
Select 10-15 deals to interview. Prioritize deals where: the stated reason is vague, the deal was large, or the loss was surprising.
Prepare a short email requesting a 15-minute conversation: 'We are trying to improve and your honest feedback would help us. This is not a sales call.'

steps.description: Interview each lost prospect using a structured protocol that makes honesty easy and avoids defensiveness.

outputs.name: interview-notes
outputs.desc: Verbatim notes from each interview, capturing the real reason, the decision process, and what would have changed the outcome

outputs.name: real-reasons
outputs.desc: The actual reason each deal was lost, as stated by the buyer (not your interpretation)

process: Open the conversation by making honesty safe: 'I appreciate you taking this call. We are genuinely trying to improve. The more honest you are, the more it helps us. Nothing you say will be taken personally.'

Ask the core questions in order: (1) Walk me through how you made this decision. (2) What were the top 3 factors? (3) Where did we fall short compared to the option you chose? (4) Was there anything we could have done differently that would have changed the outcome?
Listen without defending. When the prospect says something that stings, write it down verbatim instead of explaining why they are wrong. The instinct to defend destroys the honesty.
After each interview, record the real reason (in their words) and compare it to the stated CRM reason. The gap between the two is your data quality problem.

steps.description: Extract patterns across all interviews: the recurring themes that explain most of your losses.

outputs.name: loss-patterns
outputs.desc: The 3-5 recurring themes across the interviews, ranked by frequency

outputs.name: fixable-vs-structural
outputs.desc: Each pattern classified as fixable (can change within 90 days) or structural (requires product/market change)

process: Lay out all interview notes side by side. Look for themes that appear in 3 or more interviews. A theme in 1 interview is an opinion; a theme in 5 is a pattern.

Common patterns: 'Your product does X but does not do Y' (feature gap), 'We could not justify the price to our CFO' (value communication failure), 'Your competitor had a stronger relationship with our team' (relationship gap), 'The switching cost was too high' (migration problem).

Classify each pattern as fixable (you could address it within 90 days) or structural (it requires a product redesign, a market repositioning, or accepting the loss). Focus effort on the fixable patterns.
Rank by frequency. The pattern that appears most often is the single change that would win back the most deals.

steps.description: For each fixable pattern, design a specific change to the sales process, messaging, or product that addresses it.

outputs.name: action-plan
outputs.desc: For each fixable pattern: the specific change, who owns it, and the deadline

outputs.name: expected-win-rate-impact
outputs.desc: Estimated improvement in win rate if the top pattern is fixed

process: For each fixable pattern, design the intervention. If the pattern is 'could not justify price to CFO,' the intervention might be: create a one-page ROI calculator that the champion can hand to the CFO.

Make each intervention specific and owned. 'Improve value messaging' is not an action. 'Rewrite the proposal executive summary to lead with the dollar impact, not the feature list, by November 1, owned by [name]' is an action.
Estimate the win rate impact: if this pattern explained 30% of losses and the fix addresses it fully, your win rate could improve by up to 30% of the loss rate.
Schedule a follow-up loss analysis in 6 months to see if the patterns have shifted.

steps.description: Set up ongoing loss analysis as a quarterly practice, not a one-time exercise.

outputs.name: quarterly-schedule
outputs.desc: The ongoing schedule for loss interviews (5 interviews per quarter, 15 minutes each)

outputs.name: pattern-tracking
outputs.desc: A simple tracker showing how loss patterns change over time as interventions take effect

process: Schedule 5 loss interviews per quarter. This is enough to detect patterns without being burdensome.
Track the loss patterns quarter over quarter. The patterns you fixed should decrease in frequency. New patterns may emerge.
Share the loss analysis findings with the entire team quarterly. Sales teams that understand why they lose outperform teams that only celebrate wins.
Close the loop: when a pattern is fixed and the loss rate drops, connect the improvement to the specific intervention. This builds the habit of learning from losses.

description: Map the champion inside the prospect organization: the person who will sell for you when you are not in the room. Identify them by testing who takes action after meetings, then equip them with ammunition for internal conversations.

steps.description: Map every person involved in the buying decision and their role: decision maker, influencer, gatekeeper, end user, budget holder.

inputs.name: deal-context
inputs.desc: The deal, the prospect organization, and what you know about the people involved

inputs.name: known-contacts
inputs.desc: People you have met or communicated with so far

outputs.name: stakeholder-map
outputs.desc: Every person in the decision with their name, title, role in the decision (decision maker, influencer, gatekeeper, end user, budget holder), and your relationship strength with them

outputs.name: unknown-stakeholders
outputs.desc: Roles you know exist but have not identified the person (e.g., you know there is a budget holder but do not know who)

process: List every person you have interacted with. Assign each a role: decision maker (has final authority), influencer (shapes the decision but does not make it), gatekeeper (controls access), end user (will use the product daily), budget holder (controls the money).

Identify gaps: roles that must exist but where you do not know who holds them. The most dangerous gap is an unknown decision maker (you think you are selling to the decision maker but they actually report to someone else).

Rate your relationship strength with each person: strong (they take your calls, share internal info), medium (they are engaged but cautious), weak (they attend meetings but do not respond between them), hostile (they have objections or prefer a competitor).
The stakeholder map is the foundation. Without it, you are selling blind.

steps.description: Identify the champion by testing who takes action between meetings, not who talks the most during them.

inputs.name: stakeholder-map
inputs.desc: All people in the buying decision

outputs.name: champion-candidate
outputs.desc: The person who takes unsolicited action to advance the deal between meetings

outputs.name: champion-evidence
outputs.desc: Specific actions they have taken: scheduled follow-up meetings, shared materials internally, introduced you to other stakeholders, answered your questions proactively

process: After each meeting, note who follows up without being asked. The champion is the person who emails you a question that evening, schedules the next meeting before you ask, or shares your materials with their team without prompting.
Test by asking for a small action at the end of each meeting: 'Could you share this summary with [person]?' The champion does it. The non-champion forgets.

Do not confuse the champion with the most enthusiastic person in the room. Enthusiasm without action is not championship. The quiet person who forwards your proposal to the CFO with a note saying 'I think we should do this' is your champion.
If nobody takes action between meetings, you may not have a champion yet. Without one, the deal is at high risk.

steps.description: Equip the champion with the specific materials and arguments they need for internal conversations you are not part of.

inputs.name: stakeholder-map
inputs.desc: The other people the champion must convince

outputs.name: champion-toolkit
outputs.desc: Materials tailored for the champion to use internally: a one-page executive summary, an ROI calculation, answers to likely objections from each stakeholder

outputs.name: objection-prep
outputs.desc: The specific objections each stakeholder is likely to raise and the champion's counter-arguments

process: Ask the champion directly: 'When you present this internally, what questions will you get? What objections will [CFO/CTO/VP] raise?' The champion knows the internal dynamics better than you do.
Create materials the champion can use without modification: a one-page summary they can forward, an ROI calculation they can present, a competitive comparison they can reference.
For each likely objection from each stakeholder, give the champion a one-sentence counter-argument. The counter-argument must use the stakeholder's language and priorities, not yours.
The champion is doing your job inside the building. Make that job as easy as possible. The easier it is for them, the more likely they are to do it.

steps.description: Monitor the champion's engagement throughout the deal to detect early if they disengage or lose influence.

outputs.name: engagement-signals
outputs.desc: Positive and negative signals about the champion's engagement and internal influence

outputs.name: risk-assessment
outputs.desc: Whether the champion is still active and influential, or whether the deal needs a new champion or a different approach

process: Track positive signals: the champion responds within 24 hours, provides internal updates unprompted, introduces you to new stakeholders, asks for additional materials.
Track negative signals: response times increase, meetings are rescheduled or cancelled, the champion stops providing internal context, they stop forwarding materials.
If negative signals appear, have a direct conversation: 'I notice things have slowed down. Is there something happening internally that I should know about?' A good champion will tell you.
If the champion has lost influence (new boss, organization change, role shift), you need a new champion. The deal is not dead, but it needs a new internal advocate.

steps.description: For large deals, build multiple champions at different levels of the organization to protect against single-point-of-failure risk.

outputs.name: secondary-champion-candidates
outputs.desc: 1-2 additional people who could become champions at different levels (e.g., executive sponsor, end-user advocate)

outputs.name: multi-champion-plan
outputs.desc: How to develop relationships with secondary champions without undermining the primary one

process: For deals above a certain size, one champion is a single point of failure. If they leave, get promoted, or lose influence, the deal stalls.

Identify 1-2 potential secondary champions at different organizational levels. An executive sponsor (senior enough to override objections) and an end-user advocate (who can speak to daily value) create a three-level support structure.

Develop secondary champions carefully. The primary champion must not feel bypassed. Ask them: 'Would it be helpful if I also connected with [executive] to build support at that level?' Let the primary champion introduce you.
A deal with champions at three levels (executive, manager, end-user) is significantly more resilient than one with a single champion.

description: Mine competitor reviews for objections and talking points: read every 2-3 star review of competitors to find specific complaints your product solves. These become sales ammunition grounded in real frustration.

steps.description: Collect 2-3 star reviews of your top 3-5 competitors from every review platform.

inputs.name: review-platforms
inputs.desc: Where reviews exist (G2, Capterra, Trustpilot, Google Reviews, app stores, industry forums)

outputs.name: review-corpus
outputs.desc: 100-300 reviews rated 2-3 stars across all competitors, with the full text, rating, and date

outputs.name: review-count-by-competitor
outputs.desc: How many reviews collected per competitor

process: Focus on 2-3 star reviews. 1-star reviews are often rage-driven and unspecific. 4-5 star reviews tell you what works. 2-3 star reviews contain the most actionable complaints: specific enough to be useful, measured enough to be credible.
Collect at least 20 reviews per competitor. Fewer than 20 does not give enough data to detect patterns.
Copy the full text, not just the star rating. The value is in the specific language the reviewer uses to describe their frustration.
Note the date. Reviews older than 2 years may describe problems the competitor has since fixed.

steps.description: Extract and categorize the complaint themes across all reviews.

outputs.name: complaint-themes
outputs.desc: The 5-10 most common complaint themes across all competitors, with the count and example quotes for each

outputs.name: competitor-specific-complaints
outputs.desc: Themes that are specific to one competitor (their unique weakness)

process: Read every review and tag each complaint with a theme: pricing, support, reliability, features, ease of use, onboarding, performance, integration, billing.
Count the frequency of each theme across all reviews. A theme that appears in 40% of reviews is a structural industry problem, not just one competitor's issue.
Pull 3-5 example quotes for each theme. Use the reviewer's exact words. 'I spent 3 hours trying to set up the basic integration and gave up' is more useful than 'onboarding is bad.'

Separate universal themes (problems with every competitor) from competitor-specific themes (problems unique to one). Universal themes are positioning opportunities for your entire brand. Specific themes are competitive selling points.

steps.description: Match each complaint theme to your product's specific solution for that problem.

outputs.name: solution-matches
outputs.desc: For each complaint theme: how your product specifically solves this problem, with evidence (screenshots, data, customer quotes)

outputs.name: unaddressed-complaints
outputs.desc: Complaint themes where your product has the same problem (do NOT use these in sales conversations)

process: For each complaint theme, document exactly how your product addresses it. Be specific: 'Our onboarding takes 15 minutes, not 3 hours, because we auto-detect the integration settings.'
Provide evidence for each claim. A feature list is not evidence. A screenshot, a customer quote, or a measured metric is evidence.
Identify complaint themes where your product has the same problem. These are NOT selling points. Using them will backfire when the prospect discovers the truth.
The strongest solution matches are where the complaint is universal (every competitor has it) and your solution is unique (only you have fixed it). These are your differentiation.

steps.description: Turn the solution matches into usable sales materials: talk tracks, objection handlers, and competitive battle cards.

inputs.name: solution-matches
inputs.desc: Each complaint matched to your solution

outputs.name: talk-tracks
outputs.desc: For each top complaint theme: a 30-second talk track that names the problem (in the reviewer's words) and your solution (with evidence)

outputs.name: battle-cards
outputs.desc: One-page competitive battle cards for each competitor showing their top complaints and your corresponding strengths

process: Write a talk track for each top theme: 'One thing we hear from people switching from [competitor] is [exact reviewer quote]. We built [specific feature] to address exactly that. Here is how it works: [30-second demo or explanation].'
The talk track uses the reviewer's words, not your marketing language. When a prospect hears their own frustration described accurately, they trust you.
Create a one-page battle card for each competitor: their top 3 complaint themes, your solution for each, and the evidence. Sales reps can reference this before competitive calls.
Update the review corpus and materials quarterly. Competitors change, new reviews appear, and some complaints get fixed.

steps.description: Set up a quarterly refresh to keep the competitive intelligence current.

outputs.name: refresh-schedule
outputs.desc: Quarterly review mining calendar with specific dates and responsibilities

outputs.name: change-log
outputs.desc: Template for tracking what changed each quarter: new complaints, fixed complaints, new competitors

process: Collect new reviews quarterly. Focus on reviews from the past 3 months.
Compare new themes to the previous quarter. Are any complaint themes fading (competitor fixed it)? Are new themes emerging?
Update talk tracks and battle cards with new data. Remove talking points about problems the competitor has fixed.
Share updates with the sales team. The first 5 minutes of a quarterly sales meeting can cover: 'Here is what changed in the competitive landscape based on real customer reviews.'

description: Quantify the prospect's pain in dollars before proposing a solution. 'Our product saves time' is weak. 'You spend $36,000/year on manual reconciliation' is a number that frames the price as an investment.

steps.description: Interview the prospect to discover the specific pain: what are they doing manually, what errors occur, what opportunities are they missing?

inputs.name: prospect-context
inputs.desc: What you know about the prospect's business or situation

inputs.name: product-relevance
inputs.desc: How your product or service relates to their situation

outputs.name: pain-points
outputs.desc: 3-5 specific pain points described in the prospect's words

outputs.name: pain-evidence
outputs.desc: For each pain point: the prospect's estimate of frequency, time spent, errors caused, or opportunities lost

process: Ask open questions about the current process: 'Walk me through how you handle [the area your product addresses] today. Start from the beginning.' Let them describe it in detail.

Listen for time sinks ('it takes us about 3 hours every week'), error rates ('we probably get it wrong 10% of the time'), and missed opportunities ('by the time we have the report, the window has closed').
Do not lead the prospect to exaggerate. Ask for specifics: 'When you say it takes a long time, roughly how many hours per week? Who does it?' Specifics produce credible numbers.
Record the pain in the prospect's own words and numbers. These become the inputs for the dollar calculation.

steps.description: Convert each pain point into a dollar amount per year using the prospect's own numbers.

inputs.name: pain-evidence
inputs.desc: Frequency, time, error rates, missed opportunities

outputs.name: pain-in-dollars
outputs.desc: Each pain point converted to an annual dollar cost using a transparent formula

outputs.name: total-annual-pain
outputs.desc: Sum of all pain points in dollars per year

process: For time-based pain: hours per week x fully loaded hourly rate x 52 weeks. Use the prospect's stated hours and their approximate salary level (or ask). Example: 8 hours/week x $50/hour x 52 = $20,800/year.
For error-based pain: error rate x number of transactions x average cost per error. Example: 5% error rate x 200 transactions/month x $150/error x 12 months = $18,000/year.
For opportunity-based pain: number of missed opportunities x average value per opportunity. Example: 2 missed deals/month x $5,000 average deal x 12 months = $120,000/year.
Show your math transparently. The prospect should be able to verify every number. If they adjust a number, recalculate in real time. Their corrections make the final number more credible, not less.

steps.description: Present the quantified pain to the prospect in a way that frames your price as an investment against a larger cost.

inputs.name: total-annual-pain
inputs.desc: Total annual cost of the pain

outputs.name: pain-presentation
outputs.desc: A one-page summary showing: the pain in the prospect's words, the dollar amount, and the formula used

outputs.name: pricing-frame
outputs.desc: Your price presented as a percentage of the pain eliminated: 'This costs $X/year and addresses a $Y/year problem'

process: Present the one-page summary: 'Based on what you told me, this problem costs your organization approximately $X per year. Here is how I calculated that. [Show the formula with their numbers.]'
Let the prospect react. They may adjust the numbers up or down. Either is fine. The goal is not a precise number; the goal is a credible order of magnitude that puts your price in context.
Frame your price against the pain: 'Our product costs $12,000 per year. Based on your numbers, it addresses approximately $60,000 in annual costs. The ROI is approximately 5:1.'

Do not proceed to pricing until the prospect has agreed that the pain number is roughly correct. If they dispute it, recalculate with their corrections. The pain number must be their number, not yours.

steps.description: Create a document the champion can use to justify the purchase internally, with the quantified pain and ROI calculation.

outputs.name: internal-justification-doc
outputs.desc: A one-page document the champion can present to their CFO or decision maker, showing the pain, the cost, and the ROI

outputs.name: cfm-objection-prep
outputs.desc: Answers to the three most likely CFO objections: 'Can we do this ourselves?', 'What if the numbers are wrong?', 'Is there a cheaper option?'

process: Create the justification doc: Problem (in their words), Cost (using their numbers), Solution (what your product does), Investment (your price), Return (their numbers minus your price).
Make the document forward-ready: the champion should be able to email it to the CFO without editing. No jargon, no selling language, just the math.

Prepare the champion for three standard CFO objections: 'Can we build this ourselves?' (calculate the internal build cost and compare), 'What if these numbers are optimistic?' (show the break-even: even at 50% of the estimated pain, the ROI is still positive), 'Is there a cheaper option?' (cheaper options exist, here is what they do not include).
The goal is to make the internal sale as easy as the external one. The champion's conversation with their CFO is the real closing conversation.

description: Diagnose slow deal velocity by measuring time in each sales stage and identifying the stage where deals stall. Fix the bottleneck stage and overall velocity improves.

steps.description: Measure the average time deals spend in each stage of your sales pipeline.

inputs.name: pipeline-data
inputs.desc: Deals from the past 6-12 months with dates they entered and exited each stage

inputs.name: pipeline-stages
inputs.desc: The stages in your sales process (e.g., lead, qualified, proposal, negotiation, closed)

outputs.name: stage-times
outputs.desc: Average time in each stage (in days) for both won and lost deals

outputs.name: total-cycle-time
outputs.desc: Average total time from first contact to close (win or lose)

process: For each deal, calculate the number of days it spent in each stage. Use actual stage transition dates from your CRM, not estimates.
Calculate the average and median time per stage. The median is more useful than the average because a few very long deals can skew the average.
Calculate separately for won deals and lost deals. Deals that will be lost often linger in the pipeline longer than deals that will be won.
Identify the stage with the longest average duration. This is the bottleneck stage.

steps.description: Diagnose why deals stall in the bottleneck stage: what is happening (or not happening) that causes delays.

outputs.name: bottleneck-stage
outputs.desc: The stage where deals spend the most time

outputs.name: stall-reasons
outputs.desc: The specific reasons deals stall in this stage (missing information, slow approvals, unclear next steps, champion disengagement, competitor evaluation)

process: Look at the bottleneck stage and review 10-15 deals that spent excessive time there. What was happening? Pull CRM notes, emails, and meeting records.

Common stall reasons by stage: Qualification stalls because the salesperson cannot reach the decision maker. Proposal stalls because the prospect is comparing options. Negotiation stalls because legal review is slow. Identify which applies to your bottleneck.
Interview your sales team: 'When a deal gets stuck in [stage], what is usually the reason?' Their answers, combined with the deal-level data, reveal the pattern.

Separate stalls caused by your process (you were slow to send the proposal, you did not follow up) from stalls caused by the prospect's process (their legal team takes 30 days, their budget cycle is quarterly).

steps.description: Design an intervention that reduces time in the bottleneck stage.

outputs.name: intervention
outputs.desc: The specific change to reduce time in the bottleneck stage

outputs.name: expected-time-reduction
outputs.desc: The estimated reduction in days at the bottleneck stage

process: Match the intervention to the stall reason. If the stall is 'waiting for legal review,' the intervention might be: provide a pre-approved contract template that reduces legal review from 30 days to 5 days.
If the stall is 'prospect is comparing options,' the intervention might be: deliver the competitive comparison proactively at the start of the stage instead of waiting for the prospect to ask.
If the stall is internal (your team is slow), the intervention is a process change with a deadline commitment: 'Proposals will be delivered within 48 hours of the qualification call.'

Choose one intervention for the bottleneck stage. Do not try to fix multiple stages simultaneously. Reducing time in the bottleneck by 30% has a larger impact on total cycle time than reducing time in a non-bottleneck by 50%.

steps.description: Set up ongoing tracking of deal velocity so you can detect new bottlenecks as the pipeline evolves.

outputs.name: velocity-dashboard
outputs.desc: A dashboard showing: average time per stage (current vs baseline), total cycle time trend, and the current bottleneck stage

outputs.name: review-cadence
outputs.desc: Monthly review of velocity metrics to detect new bottlenecks

process: Build a monthly dashboard that tracks average days in each stage. Compare to the baseline established before the intervention.
Flag any stage where average time increases by more than 20% from baseline. This indicates a new or returning bottleneck.
Track total cycle time as a single metric. The goal is to reduce total cycle time while maintaining or improving win rate. Faster deals that lose more often are not an improvement.

Review monthly. As you fix one bottleneck, another stage will become the new slowest. This is expected. The cycle of identify-diagnose-intervene continues until total cycle time reaches an acceptable level.

description: Disqualify prospects before trying to qualify them. Ask early: 'Is there any reason this would not work for you?' Fast disqualification concentrates effort on prospects who will actually close.

steps.description: Define the specific criteria that make a prospect a bad fit, based on historical data about which deals close and which do not.

inputs.name: deal-history
inputs.desc: Historical deals with outcomes (won, lost, stalled)

inputs.name: product-fit
inputs.desc: What your product does well and what it does not do

outputs.name: disqualification-criteria
outputs.desc: 5-7 specific criteria that predict a deal will not close (wrong size, wrong industry, missing budget, no champion, using a competitor they are happy with, timeline too long, need a feature you do not have)

outputs.name: criteria-evidence
outputs.desc: For each criterion: the historical close rate for deals that met this criterion vs deals that did not

process: Analyze your historical deals. Group by outcome (won vs lost). Look for characteristics that are overrepresented in losses: industry, company size, deal size, buying process length, number of decision makers, stated budget.
The best disqualification criteria are the ones with the strongest predictive power: deals with this characteristic close at less than 10% vs the overall close rate of 25%.
Limit to 5-7 criteria. More than 7 and every prospect gets disqualified. The criteria should be binary (yes/no) and verifiable early in the sales process.
Include at least one behavioral criterion, not just demographic. 'The prospect does not respond to follow-ups within 5 business days' is a behavioral disqualification signal.

steps.description: Design questions that surface disqualification criteria in the first conversation, without being abrasive.

outputs.name: disqualification-questions
outputs.desc: 5-7 questions that each map to a disqualification criterion, phrased to sound helpful rather than interrogative

outputs.name: question-timing
outputs.desc: When in the first conversation to ask each question (early, but after rapport is established)

process: For each criterion, write a question that surfaces it naturally. Instead of 'Do you have budget?' ask 'What is your process for evaluating and approving new investments in this area?' The answer reveals whether budget exists without making it a yes/no gate.
Phrase questions as helpful: 'I want to make sure I do not waste your time. A few quick questions to see if this is a fit.' Most prospects appreciate efficiency.
Ask the most likely disqualification question first. If the most common reason deals fail is 'wrong company size,' ask about company size early.

Listen for both the explicit answer and the implicit signal. 'We do not really have a budget for this' is explicit. 'That is an interesting idea, we might look at that next year' is an implicit 'no budget now.'

steps.description: When a prospect hits a disqualification criterion, exit gracefully so the door stays open for the future.

outputs.name: exit-scripts
outputs.desc: Professional language for disqualifying a prospect that preserves the relationship: 'Based on what you have shared, I do not think we are the right fit right now because [specific reason]'

outputs.name: nurture-handoff
outputs.desc: How to hand disqualified prospects to a nurture sequence so they can re-enter when their situation changes

process: Be honest and specific: 'Based on what you have shared, I think [competitor/alternative] might actually be a better fit for your situation because [specific reason]. I would rather send you in the right direction than try to make something work that will not.' This builds trust.
Never disappear or go silent. An unexplained disappearance burns the bridge. A clear, honest disqualification leaves the bridge intact.
Add disqualified prospects to a low-touch nurture sequence. Their situation may change (they grow, they get budget, they fire the competitor). When it does, they should hear from you.
Track disqualification rates. If you are disqualifying more than 50% of first conversations, your lead generation is targeting too broadly. If less than 10%, your criteria may be too loose.

steps.description: Measure the time saved by early disqualification and the impact on win rate for the remaining qualified pipeline.

outputs.name: time-savings
outputs.desc: Hours per month saved by not pursuing deals that would have been lost anyway

outputs.name: win-rate-improvement
outputs.desc: The change in win rate for the qualified pipeline (expected to increase because low-probability deals are removed)

process: Calculate time saved: (number of disqualified prospects per month) x (average hours spent on a lost deal). If you disqualify 10 prospects per month and each lost deal consumed 8 hours, you save 80 hours/month.
Measure the win rate of the qualified pipeline (deals that passed disqualification). It should be higher than the overall win rate before disqualification was implemented.
Reallocate the saved time to the qualified pipeline. More time per qualified deal means better discovery, better proposals, and better follow-up, which further improves win rate.
The compounding effect: early disqualification saves time, which is reinvested in qualified deals, which improves win rate, which generates more revenue per hour of sales effort.

description: Write proposals by inversion: start with the cost of NOT buying (the status quo cost), then present your solution as the less expensive alternative. The frame shifts from 'this costs $X' to 'NOT doing this costs $Y, and Y is greater than X.'

steps.description: Calculate the total annual cost of the prospect's current approach (the status quo) using numbers from the discovery conversation.

inputs.name: discovery-notes
inputs.desc: Notes from the discovery conversation showing the prospect's current process, pain points, and the numbers they shared

outputs.name: status-quo-cost
outputs.desc: The total annual cost of the current approach: direct costs (time, errors, tools) plus indirect costs (missed opportunities, risk)

outputs.name: cost-breakdown
outputs.desc: The status quo cost broken down by category with the formula for each

process: Sum all direct costs of the current approach: labor time spent on the task, cost of errors and rework, cost of current tools or vendors, cost of manual processes.
Add indirect costs: opportunities lost because the current process is slow or inaccurate, risk exposure from errors or non-compliance, customer churn caused by slow service.
Use the prospect's own numbers wherever possible. When they said 'about 20 hours per week,' use 20. When they said 'we lose maybe 2 deals a month to slow response time,' use 2.
The total status quo cost is the number your proposal will be compared against. It is the implicit price tag of doing nothing.

steps.description: Structure the proposal to lead with the status quo cost, then introduce your solution as the path to eliminating that cost.

outputs.name: inverted-proposal
outputs.desc: The proposal structured as: (1) the cost of the current approach, (2) what your solution changes, (3) the new cost after implementation, (4) the net savings

outputs.name: executive-summary
outputs.desc: A 3-sentence executive summary that leads with the status quo cost

process: Page 1 (executive summary): 'Your current approach to [area] costs approximately $X per year. Our solution reduces that cost to approximately $Y per year. The net improvement is $Z per year, producing an ROI of N:1.'
Page 2 (status quo breakdown): show the cost breakdown from the discovery conversation, using the prospect's numbers. This page exists to establish the problem size, not to sell.
Page 3 (solution and new state): describe what changes with your product and the resulting cost structure. For each cost category, show the before and after.

Page 4 (investment and ROI): your price, the net savings, and the payback period. The price should feel small compared to the status quo cost because the proposal has spent 2 pages establishing how expensive the status quo is.

steps.description: Create a visual that makes the cost comparison impossible to miss: the status quo bar towering over the solution bar.

outputs.name: comparison-visual
outputs.desc: A bar chart or side-by-side table showing the annual status quo cost, your annual price, and the net savings - designed to make the gap immediately obvious

outputs.name: highlight-annotations
outputs.desc: Annotations on the visual that call out the key numbers

process: Create a bar chart with two bars: status quo annual cost (tall) and your annual price (short). The gap between them is the annual savings.
Use actual dollar amounts, not percentages. '$87,000 vs $12,000' is more impactful than '86% savings.'
Include a time dimension: 'Over 3 years, the status quo costs $261,000 while our solution costs $36,000.' Multi-year framing amplifies the gap.
This visual should be the most memorable element of the proposal. Decisions are made visually, and this comparison image is what the champion will remember and describe to the CFO.

steps.description: Add a section on the risk of doing nothing: what happens if the status quo continues for another 12 months.

outputs.name: do-nothing-risk
outputs.desc: The projected cost of the status quo over the next 12 months, including any trends that suggest costs are growing

outputs.name: urgency-frame
outputs.desc: A statement that frames delay as a cost: 'Every month of delay costs approximately $X'

process: Project the status quo cost forward 12 months. If any cost component is growing (more transactions, more employees, more complexity), the future cost is higher than the current cost.
Calculate the monthly cost of delay: total annual status quo cost divided by 12. 'Every month you wait costs approximately $7,250 in continued waste.'
Do not manufacture false urgency. If the cost is genuinely flat, say so. But most status quo costs grow because the underlying business grows.
Position this section as information, not pressure. 'We want you to have the full picture to make the right decision on your timeline.'
